This prospective cohort study (n=52) measured absolute concentrations of specific short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) in fecal and plasma samples from solid tumor patients treated with PD-1 inhibitors (nivolumab or pembrolizumab). Fecal samples were analyzed for acetic acid (AA), propionic acid (PA), butyric acid (BA), valeric acid (VA), and others, reported in μmol/g (e.g., median fecal PA: 172.6 μmol/g in responders vs 103.6 μmol/g in nonresponders). Plasma samples were analyzed for SCFAs including isovaleric acid (IVA), reported in μmol/g (e.g., median plasma IVA: 0.3 μmol/g in responders vs 0.0 μmol/g in nonresponders). High concentrations of fecal AA, PA, BA, VA and plasma IVA were significantly associated with longer progression-free survival (e.g., fecal PA HR 0.08, 95% CI 0.03-0.20). The study also identified dietary associations, where high frequency of mushroom intake correlated with higher fecal BA and VA and longer progression-free survival.

This study is a narrative review that details the mechanistic axes by which gut microbial metabolites, specifically short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), modulate the tumor microenvironment (TME) and immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) response. The authors describe SCFA mechanisms including G-protein-coupled receptor binding (GPR41, GPR43, GPR109a) and histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibition, which affect T-cell exhaustion and macrophage polarization. Crucially, the authors explicitly state that while physiological mucosal concentrations favor regulatory T-cell induction, the concentration-response relationship in human tumor-bearing contexts has not been characterized. The review summarizes landmark clinical studies linking microbial composition to ICI outcomes but notes these rely on 16S rRNA or metagenomics rather than metabolomic quantification. Inosine is not discussed in the supplied text.

This study identifies specific microbial metabolites mechanistically linked to ICI response, including inosine (via Bifidobacterium pseudolongum and A2A receptor on CD8+ T cells) and short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate affecting dendritic cells and T-cell memory).

The authors report that metabolomic profiling in dietary fiber studies demonstrated higher fecal butyrate and acetate levels correlating with greater intratumoral T-cell infiltration, though absolute tumor tissue concentrations were not specified in this text.

This review notes that three metabolomic studies integrated microbiome and metabolite data to predict treatment outcomes (specifically adverse events with AUC 0.963 using fecal and plasma profiles), indicating the existence of quantitative metabolite datasets in the field.

The discussion highlights the complexity of metabolite stoichiometry and immune contexture, noting that high concentrations of butyrate can suppress IL-2-dependent memory formation while acetate/propionate enhance dendritic cell fitness.
